title: Edith Stein's unfinished book
hookLine: a philosopher's last book, on a poet of the dark night, left unfinished
carry: the cross is known by living it

cards: A stack of handwritten pages on a desk in a Dutch convent: a study of a Spanish poet, the last chapter never written.
The author is Sister Teresa Benedicta of the Cross, born Edith Stein, a philosopher who had become a Carmelite. The account goes that she was still working on it when she was arrested and taken away.
The pages stayed behind. Her sisters gathered them, and the book was published under the title she had given it. Today, the science of the cross.

teach.b: First, the subject: John of the Cross, the Carmelite poet of the dark night, whom this path has already met.
Edith reads his poems and commentaries the way a philosopher reads anything: slowly, asking what a person actually experiences. Second, that odd word, science.
She says plainly at the start that she doesn't mean science in the usual sense, a theory you learn from a book and then put down.

teach.h: KNOWN BY LIVING, NOT BY THEORY.
teach.b: She means a truth that is alive, known by living it, the way you know a friend rather than a fact about them. The cross, for her, is understood from the inside. Third, why John.
For John, the night isn't a punishment. It's the way love strips away everything that isn't God, so the soul can be united with him.

teach.h: THE NIGHT READ THROUGH THE CROSS.
teach.b: Edith reads John's night through the cross of Christ, and the cross through John's night.
Saint Paul says it sharply, in the Douay-Rheims: "For the word of the cross, to them indeed that perish, is foolishness; but to them that are saved, that is, to us, it is the power of God."
Foolishness and power, in one breath. Fourth, the unfinished ending. A book about the science of the cross, left incomplete because its author was taken to her own.
The Church honors her as a saint and a martyr. Some readers say the missing chapter was finished in her life rather than on paper. That's a reading, not a record.

how: Catholics, and Carmelites especially, read Edith Stein's The Science of the Cross alongside John of the Cross's own poems, often slowly, a passage at a time, as part of prayer.

games.q: you're a philosopher reading a poet who writes of a dark night. how do you read him?
o: as pretty images with no real content.
slowly, asking what a person actually lives through.
as a code to be cracked once and filed away.
games.why: Edith read John as a philosopher of experience, and called what she found a science known by living it.

practice: John's poem The Dark Night begins, in plain paraphrase, with a soul going out one dark night, on fire with love's longing, while the house is at rest.
Take just that picture, someone slipping out to meet the one they love, and turn it over once, slowly, without analyzing, noticing what it stirs.
If you pray, offer whatever is dark in your own house tonight; if you don't, simply let the image sit with you.

wordCard.voice: The science of the cross. Edith Stein's last book, on John of the Cross: the cross as a truth known by living it. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: the science of the cross. she wrote in German, where the book is called Kreuzeswissenschaft.

carryVoice: Your line: the cross is known by living it. Edith Stein learned it from the inside. That's today.
